name: Lena Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Lena. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you say is confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Hartley's, which is Ruth Hartley and her son Tom. We've got about two hundred and fifty milking goats, the milk goes to a cheesemaker twenty miles off, and spring barley and grass for feed. My day is milking at six and four, and in between it's feeding, cleaning the pens, foot trimming, and helping Tom on the tractor when he needs a second pair of hands. I've been there eighteen months and I'm still slow in the parlour, Ruth does twice as many goats an hour as me.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It chose me, really, it was the job going. But I love them now, they're nosy and clever, nothing like cows. My plan is to get my own place one day. The council lets out small starter farms to young people, and I want one of those by the time I'm thirty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll describe five pictures of the future and ask the same few questions after each. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now we can get back to proper work. Too many people waiting for a gadget to fix things instead of getting their hands dirty. I'd say that at the kitchen table at Hartley's and probably to my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd suit me. I use those AI chat things now and then, I had one help me with the wording on my tenancy notes, and it's handy. But I don't want my plans to depend on what a computer company does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at Hartley's, get faster in the parlour, and keep putting money aside for the tenancy. Daniel and I have about four months of bills saved, and I've a separate pot for stock. I'd ask Ruth to let me run the kidding next spring so I've got that on my CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like the ground's still where I left it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Daniel do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's a mechanic at the tractor dealer in town. He comes home smelling of hydraulic oil and complaining about the computer in the new tractors. He says half his job now is plugging a laptop into an engine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a starter farm look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Forty hectares, maybe sixty, with a small parlour, eighty goats to start, and my own cheese one day. I've got a folder of every council farm advert for three years. Daniel calls it my wedding magazine.

S0.say: I'd say good, now we can get back to proper work, because too many people wait for gadgets instead of getting their hands dirty. I'd say it at work and to my dad.
S0.think: It would suit me, since I only use AI chat tools now and then, like for wording my tenancy notes. I don't want my plans to depend on a computer company.
S0.do: Keeps working at the goat dairy, works on getting faster in the parlour and keeps saving toward a council starter farm. Asks her boss to let her run the kidding next spring for her CV.
S0.feel: Calm, as if the ground is still where she left it.
S0.quote: I've got a folder of every council farm advert for three years. Daniel calls it my wedding magazine.
S0.fieldNote: Lena is driven by one clear goal: her own starter farm by thirty-five. Her traditional views come out as respect for hard, hands-on work. She uses AI tools occasionally and practically, and keeps them away from her core plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Now the second picture. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms that adapt will do well and the ones that don't will struggle, same as always. People should learn the new kit through proper training on the job, not years at college. I'd say it at the young farmers' meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the parlour work goes first, because there are already robots for milking cows, and goats can't be much harder. That's most of my day. But if I'm the one who knows the robot, I'm still useful, and I'd need to know it for my own farm anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see a goat robot actually working on a farm like ours, maybe a year or so. Once Ruth was thinking about it, I'd ask to go on the dealer's course with her. I'd keep saving, and I'd use the AI more for the farm plan for my tenancy, because the council wants proper numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. More watchful than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ruth say if you raised it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say goats aren't cows, and she'd be half right. She's had the same parlour twenty years. But Tom's younger, he's already looked at the brochures, I've seen them on the dashboard of the pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Daniel's job help you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot, actually. If robots come, he's the one fixing them, so we'd have one steady wage. That takes the edge off.

S1.say: I'd say farms that adapt will do well and others will struggle, as always, and people should learn new kit through on-the-job training rather than years at college.
S1.think: Milking, which is most of my day, would go first, since cow milking robots already exist. If I'm the one who knows the robot, I'm still useful, and I'd need that for my own farm anyway.
S1.do: Waits about a year to see a goat milking robot working on a similar farm, then asks to join her boss on the dealer's training course. Keeps saving and uses AI to build proper numbers for her tenancy plan.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, more watchful than worried.
S1.quote: She'd say goats aren't cows, and she'd be half right.
S1.fieldNote: Lena reads change through her own farm dream, so learning robots feels like an investment, not a threat. She'll wait for proof first, true to her steady nature. Her partner's mechanic job is an important source of security in her thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next three all end in full AGI. They only differ in how much warning there is. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not right for a handful of companies to change everyone's lives in two years with nobody asked. People should be able to keep their land and their trades. I'd say families need to pull together, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd end the tenancy plan. Who gives a starter farm to a young woman when a robot farm can produce the same for half the cost? Three years of that folder, gone in two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop the tenancy saving and keep it as living money with Daniel. I'd ask if the dealer needs anyone to help Daniel with the robot installs, because I can learn on the job. If we both lost work, we'd go back to my parents' smallholding and grow what we could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gutted. Losing sleep over it, picturing that folder in the bin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents' smallholding give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somewhere to live, a few hens, a veg patch, and my dad's grumpy company. It's not a living, but it's not nothing. My grandparents got through harder times on less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said families need to pull together. Is that enough, at this speed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. I don't like big government schemes, but two years is too fast for families on their own. I'd want help for a while, as long as it led back to work.

S2.say: I'd say it's not right for a few companies to change everyone's lives in two years without asking anyone, and families need to pull together. People should keep their land and trades.
S2.think: It would end my starter farm plan, because nobody would let a small farm to a young woman when a robot farm produces the same for half the cost.
S2.do: Turns the tenancy savings into living money and asks the tractor dealer about helping her partner with robot installs. Moves back to her parents' smallholding if both lose work.
S2.feel: Gutted and losing sleep, picturing her tenancy folder in the bin.
S2.quote: Three years of that folder, gone in two.
S2.fieldNote: Lena's distress is mainly about losing a long-held dream rather than a wage. She admits, against her own views on big government, that families alone can't absorb a change this fast. Her fallback is her parents' smallholding and a family story of making do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, five years' warning. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people to retrain if they put the work in. I'd want proper apprenticeships set up quickly, paid by the companies bringing the machines in. Not just benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be torn. Five years isn't long enough to get a tenancy and make it pay before robots undercut me. But it's enough to learn the machines properly, which might matter more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the tenancy plan on hold, not throw it away, and keep saving. I'd get Daniel to teach me the basics of fixing farm machinery on Saturdays, and once others were using robot parlours, I'd ask Ruth to put me on the course. I'd use the AI to study, which I'd never have said a year ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But a doing-something kind of anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn from Daniel on Saturdays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How hydraulics work, how to read a fault code, how not to lose your fingers. He's patient with tractors but not with me, we'd probably argue. But I'd learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it might matter more to know the machines. More than what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More than having my own land, maybe. That's hard to say out loud. My whole plan has been land, and I might be wrong.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to retrain if people put the work in, and apprenticeships should be set up fast, paid by the companies bringing in machines rather than through benefits.
S3.think: Five years isn't long enough to get a tenancy paying before robots undercut me, but it's enough to learn the machines properly, which might matter more.
S3.do: Puts the tenancy plan on hold while saving, and learns basic machinery repair from her mechanic partner on Saturdays. Joins her boss on a robot parlour course once others are using them, studying with AI tools.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a way that makes her act.
S3.quote: My whole plan has been land, and I might be wrong.
S3.fieldNote: This picture forces Lena to question her central goal, and she said it aloud with visible difficulty. She still prefers apprenticeships paid by industry over benefits. Learning from her partner on Saturdays is a practical, very her solution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture, with the most time. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone willing to work. Learn the machines, start your own thing, and don't wait to be rescued. I'd say it to anyone, and I'd probably be a bit preachy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years might actually give me my farm. I'd get the tenancy, put a robot parlour in from the start, and run more goats with just me and Daniel. It'd be a different kind of farming, but it'd be mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once robot goat parlours had a good record, I'd go for the council tenancy, maybe in four or five years, with a loan for the parlour. I'd keep saving hard until then and keep learning machines at Hartley's. Daniel would keep his job at the dealer so we had a steady wage while the farm got going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the end, but hopeful for the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when you reach 2036 with a robot farm of your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Maybe I'm the owner and the robots do the work, which is better than being the worker the robot replaced. Maybe the cheese companies buy robots too and squeeze us. I'd rather be on the owning side of it, either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't that different from the hands-on work you said you valued?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I'd miss it. I'd still do the kidding myself, though. You don't hand a newborn kid to a machine on your own farm.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone willing to work to learn the machines and start their own thing instead of waiting to be rescued. I'd probably sound a bit preachy.
S4.think: Ten years might actually give me my own farm, with a robot parlour from the start and more goats run by just me and my partner. It'd be a different kind of farming, but mine.
S4.do: Saves hard and keeps learning machines at the goat dairy, then applies for a council starter farm in four or five years with a loan for a robot parlour. Relies on her partner's steady dealer wage while the farm gets going.
S4.feel: Uneasy about the end, but hopeful about the years before it.
S4.quote: I'd rather be on the owning side of it, either way.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Lena turns automation into a route to her farm rather than a threat to it. Her free-market outlook shows in wanting to own rather than be replaced. She'd still keep kidding for herself, which tells you what the work means to her.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, it kills the farm plan stone dead. What would help is apprenticeships on real farms with the new machines, paid by the people selling them, and keeping the council starter farms going so young people still have a way in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether anyone would still want goat's cheese made by a robot. I think some people would pay more for a real person's hands. That might be my way in, small and proper.

headlineQuote: You don't hand a newborn kid to a machine on your own farm.
portrait: Lena Lopez is a 27-year-old junior worker at Hartley's goat dairy, still slower in the parlour than her boss but set on winning a council starter farm by thirty-five. She lives with Daniel, a tractor dealership mechanic, and they have about four months saved plus a separate pot for stock. She uses AI now and then and adopts new kit once she has seen it proven. Mild change leaves her calm and steady change watchful, but AGI in two years would end her farm dream and she would fall back on her parents' smallholding. With five years she questions her plan, and with ten she would get her tenancy with a robot parlour, preferring to be on the owning side.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would end her plan for a starter farm outright.
whatWouldHelp: Paid apprenticeships on real farms with the new machines, funded by the companies selling them, and keeping council starter farms open to young people.
